insert.heading: Background
paragraphs: Priya Nair, an engineer, founded Lumen Bikes Ltd in Sheffield in 2016. Lumen designs and assembles premium electric bikes (e-bikes). Its bikes are lighter than most rivals' and their batteries last longer. Every frame carries a seven-year warranty. Lumen sells directly to customers online and through 40 independent bike shops.

The average Lumen e-bike sells for £2 800, compared with around £1 200 for mass-market e-bikes sold by large retailers. Priya has always said: 'We will never be the cheapest. Our customers pay for quality, design and the knowledge that their bike was built in Britain.'

Demand for e-bikes has grown rapidly as commuters look for alternatives to cars and public transport. Lumen's revenue has risen from £4.1m in 2021 to £14.8m in 2024, and the number of employees has grown from 38 to 112.

insert.heading: Culture and leadership
paragraphs: Priya describes her leadership style as democratic. The structure is flat: there are only three levels of hierarchy. Production teams decide how to organise their own work, and every engineer can spend 10% of their time on their own development projects. Lumen's most successful product, the 'Fold-Go' folding e-bike, began as one engineer's side project. Staff turnover is low and the business regularly wins 'best place to work' awards.
Some managers believe that, as Lumen grows, it will need more formal procedures. Priya disagrees: 'Rules kill ideas.'

insert.heading: Battery supply
paragraphs: Batteries make up 35% of the cost of Lumen's components. Lumen buys all of its batteries from Voltcell Ltd, a specialist supplier in Wales, which also supplies three of Lumen's competitors. In 2024 Voltcell raised its prices by 12%, and late deliveries forced Lumen to stop production for six weeks.
Voltcell's owner is retiring and has offered to sell the business to Lumen for £6.5m.

insert.heading: The decision
paragraphs: Option 1: Lumen buys Voltcell for £6.5m. This would be financed by selling a 30% stake in Lumen to a venture capital firm for £4.5m, with the remaining £2m from a bank loan. Voltcell would continue to supply Lumen's competitors.

Option 2: Lumen signs a five-year supply contract with Hanjin, a large South Korean battery manufacturer. Hanjin's prices would be 8% below Voltcell's current prices and fixed in US dollars for five years. Lead time would be 10 weeks, compared with 2 weeks from Voltcell, and Lumen must order at least 1 500 batteries each quarter.

insert.heading: The cargo bike launch
paragraphs: Lumen plans to launch a new cargo e-bike, designed for families and delivery businesses, in 15 weeks' time. A new production line is needed. The planned activities are shown in Appendix C.

insert.heading: Background
paragraphs: Harbour & Hale plc (H&H) was founded in 1952 and has 180 clothing stores on UK high streets. It sells mid-priced women's and men's clothing to customers aged 35 to 60. For decades H&H was known for reliable quality and good customer service.

Over the last five years, H&H's market share has fallen steadily. Online-only retailers offer wider ranges and faster delivery, while discount chains offer lower prices. Footfall on many high streets has fallen. H&H launched a website in 2016, but it is slow and has few features. Online sales are 18% of H&H's revenue, compared with 38% for the clothing market as a whole.

insert.heading: New leadership
paragraphs: In 2024 H&H's long-serving chief executive retired. His successor, Marcus Bell, joined from an online retailer. He said: 'For too long this business has made small changes while our customers changed completely.'

Marcus has announced 'Project Renew': 60 stores will close, with 1 400 redundancies; £40m will be invested in an automated distribution centre to support online sales; and the brand will be relaunched to appeal to customers aged 25 to 45.

Institutional shareholders welcomed the plan and the share price rose 9%. The trade union representing shop workers has threatened strike action. Many store managers have worked for H&H for more than 20 years and do not trust the new management team.

insert.heading: The distribution centre
paragraphs: The distribution centre would allow next-day delivery across the UK. H&H's finance director has prepared the forecasts in Appendix C. She points out that the forecasts assume online sales will double within three years.

insert.heading: Background
paragraphs: Tom and Ama Mensah set up GreenRoot Organics Ltd in 2012 on a 120-acre farm in Herefordshire. GreenRoot grows organic vegetables and delivers weekly vegetable boxes to 4 200 subscribers in the West Midlands. Its mission is 'Good food, fairly grown'.

GreenRoot employs 46 people, including 12 adults with learning disabilities who work in its packing shed through a supported-employment scheme. Staff are paid at least the Real Living Wage. Tom and Ama reinvest about 80% of profits in the farm and the local community.

insert.heading: A supermarket contract
paragraphs: A regional supermarket chain has offered GreenRoot a one-year contract to supply 200 tonnes of organic carrots and potatoes. The supermarket would pay 60 days after delivery. GreenRoot's spare land could produce only 150 tonnes; the remaining 50 tonnes would have to come from land currently used to grow vegetables for the boxes.

insert.heading: Growth options
paragraphs: Tom and Ama want GreenRoot to grow so that it can employ more people from the supported-employment scheme. They are considering two options.
Option 1: open three GreenRoot farm shops in nearby towns. This would be financed by raising £600 000 through crowd funding, offering investors 6% interest a year for five years.

Option 2: franchise the GreenRoot veg-box model to other organic farms across the UK. Each franchisee would pay a £20 000 fee and 6% of revenue, and would have to follow GreenRoot's employment and sourcing standards.

insert.heading: Background
paragraphs: Jordan Reid founded Apex Arena Ltd in 2019 at the age of 23. Apex runs esports tournaments - competitive video-gaming events - in a converted warehouse in Manchester that holds 2 000 spectators. Every event is also streamed online. Apex earns revenue from tickets, sponsorship and advertising on its streams.

Apex has grown quickly. Revenue rose from £0.4m in 2020 to £3.6m in 2024. Jordan makes almost every important decision himself, often very quickly. He says: 'In this industry, if you wait for a report, someone else has already done it.' Apex was the first UK organiser to use virtual-reality viewing for online audiences.

insert.heading: People
paragraphs: Apex has 24 full-time staff and about 150 event staff on zero-hours contracts, who work as stewards, technicians and caterers at events. Event staff turnover is high (see Appendix B). Several full-time managers have left, complaining that Jordan does not let them make decisions.

insert.heading: The Northern Showdown
paragraphs: Apex is planning its biggest event yet, the 'Northern Showdown'. Jordan must decide whether to hold it in person in a hired 10 000-seat arena or as an online-only event. The forecasts are shown in Appendix A.

insert.heading: A new arena
paragraphs: Jordan wants to build Apex's own 5 000-seat arena at a cost of £3m. He is considering two ways of financing it.
Option 1: venture capital. A venture capital firm would invest £3m in return for 35% of Apex's shares and two seats on the board.
Option 2: a £3m bank loan at 8% interest a year, repayable over 10 years and secured on Apex's assets.
